entry.title: How I Built a 50-State US Statutory Probate Calculator with Astro and Tailwind CSS
entry.summary: Navigating estate administration and probate in the US is notoriously opaque. Every state enforces different legal frameworks—from statutory attorney fee caps to tiered executor commissions and county court fees. To solve this, I built US Probate Calculator, a fast, 100% free web utility designed to calculate statutory probate and estate settlement costs across all 50 US states with zero tracking and no paywalls. I kept the stack lightweight and static for fast global loading speeds: Framework: Astro — Selected for zero-JS by default, allowing blazing-fast static page generation. Styling: Tailwind CSS — Fast, responsive, utility-first styling for a clean financial tool UI. Hosting & CDN: Cloudflare Pages — Edge network delivery with built-in SSL and near-instant load times. The primary complexity was translating disparate legal codes into consistent client-side mathematical models: California: Sliding statutory attorney/executor scale under California Probate Code § 10810 (4% of the first $100k, 3% of next $100k, 2% of next $800k, 1% of next $9M). New York: Tiered commission schedule under SCPA § 2307 (5% on first $100k, decreasing incrementally for larger estates). Florida: Statutory percentage schedules on gross estate values under Florida Statutes § 733.6171. Instead of heavy server-side processing or backend database calls, the calculation engine runs entirely on the client, ensuring total user privacy and immediate responsiveness. You can test the tool live here: usprobatecalculator.com I'd love to get your thoughts on the UI/UX, performance optimizations, or any edge cases in legal-tech calculation tools!

entry.title: Your AI Agent Needs a Cancellation Contract, Not Just a Stop Button
entry.summary: A stop button is not a cancellation protocol. In a toy agent, “stop” can mean setting a boolean and waiting for the loop to exit. In a real agent, work may already be queued, claimed by another worker, inside a browser session, or waiting for an outbound side effect. If cancellation is not represented as durable state, a restart can resurrect work the operator thought they stopped. The useful question is not “did the process receive SIGTERM?” It is: Can every layer prove whether this run may still start work, whether in-flight work must finish, and what happened to side effects that were interrupted? This article turns cancellation into a small contract you can test. Keep cancellation separate from process liveness. A worker can be alive while its run is cancelled, and a worker can die bef…
